articles.title: Lack of water storage is an urgent national security issue | Letters
articles.description: Readers respond to the crisis facing Britain caused by the lack of reservoir capacity and hotter summers Your reporters came up with a good list of urgent climate policies in response to Andy Burnham’s somewhat surreal statement focusing on the sale of disposable barbecues following a Cobra meeting ( From grey water to cool spaces: 10 climate crisis policies Britain needs right now, 12 August ), but they missed out the No 1 issue: the UK’s water-storage capacity. It is blindingly obvious that we need to dramatically and rapidly increase water storage. The current plans to fast-track the building of nine reservoirs by 2050 might be speedy by the standards of UK infrastructure delivery projects, but they may well have been overtaken by climate change trends. Continue reading...

articles.title: Ministers are in denial about the scale of the crises we face | Letter
articles.description: Having just 20 Defra staff working on climate adaptations show the government is not taking the challenges of heatwaves, wildfires and droughts seriously, writes Dr Amy McDonnell This ( Just 20 of 6,600 Defra staff working on climate adaptation amid drought and wildfires, 12 August ) is a shocking revelation from a government that has repeatedly assured us it understands the risk of the breakdown of nature and climate. Clearly not. Families forced to deal with school closures , hospitals having to cancel appointments , wildfires continuing to tear through the country, and, so far, more than 2,700 deaths recorded from extreme heat. And yet adaptation remains a tiny corner of one department. Continue reading...

articles.title: World: Locust Watch: Seasonal precipitation predictions in the Desert Locust summer and winter breeding areas (September 2026 - February 2027) (19 August 2026)
articles.description: Countries: World, Algeria, Chad, Djibouti, Egypt, Eritrea, Ethiopia, India, Iran (Islamic Republic of), Libya, Mali, Mauritania, Morocco, Niger, Oman, Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, Somalia, Sudan, Tunisia, Yemen Source: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations Please refer to the attached file. The rapid intensification of El Niño has continued in the recent weeks, and the episode is already the strongest on record for this time of year, while the positive Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD) is expected to persist in the coming months. In September, above-normal rainfall is forecast from northern Africa to the central Middle East, with wetter conditions also expected in eastern Ethiopia and Somalia due to the positive IOD. A dry signal may remain over India and Pakistan toward the close of the monsoon season. During October and November, the El Niño-related wet signal is expected to expand across northern and eastern Africa and the Middle East. Interior eastern Africa, the southern Arabian Peninsula, and Pakistan are likely to become wetter than normal. However, northwestern Africa may turn drier than normal by November. Overall, the forecast is consistent with rainfall patterns observed during previous strong El Niño events, with generally good model agreement. Some uncertainty remains over the northern Sahel and the strength of the IOD.

articles.title: Colombia: Addendum to the Humanitarian Response Plan - Earthquake August, 2026
articles.description: Country: Colombia Source: UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs Please refer to the attached file. 1. Situation Overview On 10 August 2026, a magnitude 7.4 earthquake struck Colombia, with its epicentre in San José del Palmar, Chocó department, severely affecting the central and western regions of the country. The earthquake occurred at 7:34 a.m. and was followed by sustained seismic activity. As of 12 August, 103 aftershocks had been recorded, including six with a magnitude greater than 3 and one with a magnitude greater than 4, all located in San José del Palmar. The most severe impacts have been concentrated in the departments of Risaralda, Valle del Cauca, Chocó, and Caldas, with additional damage reported in Antioquia, Quindío, Cundinamarca, Huila, Tolima, Cauca, Putumayo, Norte de Santander, and Bolívar, bringing the total reported impact area to 15 departments and 472 municipalities. The earthquake has caused significant loss of life, displacement risks, and substantial damage to housing and essential infrastructure. According to official data, at least 186,182 people, equivalent to 121,470 families, have been affected, including people who have died, been injured, or gone missing, as well as people whose homes, services, and livelihoods have been disrupted. According to the most recent reports as of 17 August, 304 people had lost their lives and 4,400 had been injured. Damage to housing is extensive: 134.341 homes have been affected and 29.554 have been destroyed, leaving many families without safe conditions to return home and increasing needs for temporary shelter, essential household items, water, and protection services. The impact extends beyond housing and affects the public services that communities depend on to recover and stabilize their living conditions. Reports indicate that 267 residential buildings collapsed. In addition, 3,443 educational institutions, 303 health facilities, and 3.905 community centres have been affected, while 86 water supply systems have sustained damage. Additionally, 413 roads have been affected across the country. Electricity, safe water, health, and connectivity services remain disrupted or are functioning intermittently in several cities. These impacts are slowing assessments, hindering access to affected areas, and increasing risks for families already exposed to aftershocks, unsafe structures, and limited access to basic services. Response operations began immediately under the leadership of the National Government and the National Disaster Risk Management System (SNGRD). Search and rescue activities remain ongoing and have enabled the rescue of 338 people, while authorities continue to provide immediate assistance and consolidate information through the Crisis Room. The National Disaster Management Committee is coordinating actions with national, departmental, and municipal entities, and Unified Command Posts (PMUs) remain active to monitor impacts, prioritize needs, and guide operational decisions. Humanitarian partners are rapidly scaling up complementary support to address the most urgent gaps in the Government-led response. United Nations agencies and international, national, and local nongovernmental organizations have begun pre-positioning capacities and deploying teams to the most affected areas, particularly Quibdó, Cali and Buenaventura, Risaralda, and Caldas. The Health; Shelter and Settlements; Water, Sanitation and Hygiene; Food Security; Protection; and Education clusters of the Humanitarian Country Team have been activated and are coordinating sectoral response efforts with national and local counterparts. Rapid assessments continue to expand in order to clarify needs and guide response priorities. Humanitarian partners continue deploying teams, pre-positioning capacities, and supporting sectoral analyses in the most affected areas, while significant information gaps persist in rural and hard-to-reach municipalities. In addition to the earthquake, communities in Cauca department are facing humanitarian impacts related to gas and ash emissions resulting from increased volcanic activity at the Puracé volcano. Likewise, in Casanare department, severe flooding has affected more than 40,000 people over the past month. This situation is compounded by wildfires in some areas as part of the drought that is beginning to emerge in the context of the development of the El Niño phenomenon. Separately, public security force operations have increased under the new government’s security policy, mainly in departments that are generating a double humanitarian impact for some communities, particularly in the Pacific region of the country. Given the scale and severity of the emergency, additional resources are being mobilized by humanitarian donors to enable a rapid, multisectoral response focused on saving lives and addressing the most immediate needs. In support of the initial response, the Emergency Relief Coordinator, Tom Fletcher, announced a USD 5 million allocation from the Central Emergency Response Fund (CERF). These funds will help humanitarian partners strengthen urgent assistance while assessments continue and response priorities are adjusted in coordination with national authorities.
